title: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014
short_title: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Act to make the regulator more efficient and reduce red tape for universities.

It would let the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency extend registration or accreditation periods on its own, give the minister more power to direct the agency and set its fees, and remove the requirement for a fixed number of commissioners.
All current commissioners would lose their positions 21 days after the bill becomes law for the chief commissioner and three months after for others, and they could reapply for the new roles.
changes: Refines the agency's functions to focus on provider registration and course accreditation.
Enables the agency to extend registration or accreditation periods on its own initiative.
Enhances delegation powers to allow internal review of decisions instead of going to the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.
Improves the minister's ability to give general directions and allows a specific direction on fees the agency charges.
Requires the agency to seek the minister's approval before changing fees.
Removes requirements to appoint a specific number of commissioners and separates the roles of chief commissioner and chief executive officer.
summary.affected: The Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency, higher education institutions, and current commissioners are affected.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014, which removes TEQSA's sector-wide quality assessment function, lets it delegate decisions to staff, and gives the minister flexibility over the number of commissioners appointed to reduce red tape on higher education providers.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: Moved a second reading amendment to the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014, arguing the government has not adequately responded to the Review of Higher Education Regulation, failed to show how the sector's international reputation would be protected, and allowed insufficient time for consultation.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA Amendment Bill implementing all 11 recommendations of the Lee Dow and Braithwaite review, saying it would let the regulator delegate decisions to speed up its backlog of provider re-registration and course accreditation applications and give providers an internal review option before appealing to the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Warned against sacrificing university quality assurance for the sake of cutting red tape, citing the Council of International Students Australia president's criticism of teaching standards and noting the University of Melbourne fell six places to 34th in the latest Times Higher Education world rankings while Singapore rose to 23rd.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA amendment bill for finally giving the regulator an internal review process instead of requiring costly Administrative Appeals Tribunal appeals, criticised Labor's Excellence in Research in Australia policy as a failure, and proposed research funding reforms including removing the 30 per cent outside-funding requirement for CSIRO and lifting Australian Research Council administrative funding from under two per cent to about five per cent.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Warned that cutting red tape must not come at the expense of quality, citing La Trobe University's announcement of 350 job cuts in Bendigo, representing 15 per cent of its workforce, and said international education already sustains over 100,000 jobs and generates more than $15 billion a year as the sector's fourth largest export earner.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA amendment bill, noting the previous Labor government cut $1.5 billion from higher education and introduced more than 18,000 regulations by 2012 while repealing only 86, quoted Universities Australia's praise for the minister's swift acceptance of all 11 review recommendations, and cited Canning College in his electorate, whose diploma program sending about 100 international students a year to two universities was forced to close after a TEQSA ruling.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Discussed the TEQSA amendment bill's origins in the Bradley review's 46 recommendations, criticised the lack of consultation with states and territories before the bill's introduction, stressed the importance of regional universities like Charles Darwin University, which has around 7,000 students, and called on the government to fund a full medical degree program through Flinders University based in Alice Springs.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Laming
speeches.brief: Supported the bill while detailing his unsuccessful efforts to get TEQSA to investigate a 2010 University of Queensland medical admissions scandal involving the vice-chancellor's daughter, which was eventually probed by a six-person Crime and Misconduct Commission panel, and said the university, which receives about $1 billion in public funding annually, allowed senior officials responsible to retire quietly on salaries between $500,000 and $1 million.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA amendment bill, citing education as Australia's third-largest export earner worth almost $16 billion in 2010-11, highlighted Cochlear's $800 million to $900 million annual revenue built on Australian research, and quoted the former Dean of UNSW Law describing TEQSA's previous approach as overreaching, excessive and ill-informed, including a requirement forcing law schools to add an extra year of study for honours degrees.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014, saying it implements a review by Professor Kwong Lee Dow and Professor Valerie Braithwaite by narrowing the agency's focus to provider registration and course accreditation and removing its quality assessment function.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA Amendment Bill while highlighting rural education disadvantage, saying 35.5 per cent of Goulburn-Murray school leavers deferred university compared with 21 per cent across Victoria, said La Trobe University was withdrawing courses and jobs from its Bendigo campus, and cited teenage unemployment of 32.5 per cent in Greater Shepparton against 30 per cent across Victoria.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the TEQSA Amendment Bill, noting Australia's university sector grew from 6 universities and 14,236 students under Menzies in 1939 to 16 universities and 91,272 students by 1966 and today employs over 107,000 people generating more than $20 billion in revenue, and read a letter from University of Western Sydney Vice-Chancellor Barney Glover supporting the changes.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Summed up debate on the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Amendment Bill 2014, saying the opposition was not opposing it, that it implements the August 2013 independent Review of higher education regulation by removing TEQSA's quality assessment function, and that current commissioner appointments will be curtailed to 21 days after royal assent for the chief commissioner and three months for other commissioners.
